0.title: The Truth That Sets You Free
0.essay:
Some lies shout. The most dangerous ones whisper, in a voice that sounds like your own. You hear it in front of the mirror, at the end of an exhausting day, when an old memory surfaces, or when you sit in church and wonder whether there is really a place for you. This study is about those whispers, and about the truth that answers them.

The oldest whisper

The first lie in the Bible came as a question: “Did God actually say …?” (Genesis 3:1). It did not deny God outright. It made him seem a little less good, a little less generous, than he is. Most of the lies we tell ourselves work the same way: half-truths, bent just enough to lead us away from God’s love. Jesus called the devil “a liar and the father of lies” (John 8:44). But he also made a promise: “you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free” (John 8:32). And he said of himself, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). The truth that frees is not only a set of facts. It is a Person who loves us.

Why women?

The lies in this study are ones that women very often tell themselves. Men believe many of them too, and some women will not recognise themselves in every chapter. These are tendencies, not rules. Its companion study, Lies Men Tell Themselves, takes up the lies that men most often believe.

This study is for every woman: single, married, widowed or divorced; working outside the home, at home, or both; with children or without; nineteen or ninety. None of these callings makes a woman more or less precious to God.

How each chapter works

Each chapter names one or two lies in a woman’s own words, asks why they are so believable, answers them from Scripture, and listens for what Christ says to her. Where other studies, such as Biblical Womanhood and Shame, go deeper, we will point to them.

The chapters

“My Worth Is in the Mirror”; “It All Depends on Me”; “Not Enough, and Too Much”; “My Past Disqualifies Me”; “Second-Class, and Not Yet Complete”; and Truth for Every Day.

For reflection

Which sentence about yourself do you hear most often in your own head? Where do you think you first learned it?

1.title: “My Worth Is in the Mirror”
1.essay:
Few lies are learned so early or repeated so often. Before a girl can read, she has usually noticed that looks get noticed. By the time she is grown, many women cannot pass a mirror or open a photograph without a quick verdict: too much here, not enough there, older than last year.

The lie in her own words

It rarely sounds like a doctrine. It sounds like this. “I can’t go out looking like this.” “If I lost the weight, I’d finally feel all right.” “He would love me more if I looked like her.” “I used to be pretty.” It lives in the photograph quietly deleted, the compliment replayed for a week, the dread of a birthday, the body after pregnancy, illness, surgery or simply the years. Underneath them all is one sentence: my worth depends on how I look.

Why it is so believable

Like most lies, this one leans on something true. Beauty is real, and it is good. God made a world full of it and called it “very good” (Genesis 1:31). Scripture is not embarrassed to say that Sarah, Rachel and Esther were beautiful. And it is simply true that our world rewards appearance. Women are judged on their looks far more than men, in workplaces, on screens and sometimes in churches. You are not imagining that pressure.

The lie is not that beauty matters. It is that beauty measures you. And comparison sharpens it, because every photograph of another woman becomes a scoreboard. The study Envy & Comparison deals with that habit more fully.

What God looks at

When Samuel was sure he had found Israel’s next king by his height and bearing, God corrected him: “For the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).

Peter writes to women: “Do not let your adorning be external … but let your adorning be the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God’s sight is very precious” (1 Peter 3:3–4). He is not banning jewellery or a good haircut. He is saying where a woman’s real adornment lies, and therefore where she can rest. Outward beauty is perishable. The beauty God grows in a heart that trusts him is not. “Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised” (Proverbs 31:30). “Vain” here means fleeting, a breath. It is lovely, and it does not last.

Paul knew bodies age: “Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16). For a Christian woman, growing older is not only loss. Something is being made new on the inside.

Made, not graded

“So God created man in his own image … male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27). Your body is not a project to be graded. It is a gift from a Maker who took care over it. “I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made” (Psalm 139:14). That is true of the body you have today, with its scars and its years, not only of the one you wish you had.

For some women this struggle goes beyond vanity or insecurity. If thoughts about food, weight or shape have begun to rule your days, or you are restricting, bingeing or purging, please speak to a doctor soon. That is not a failure of faith. The study Eating Disorders is written for you and for those who love you.

An example

A school administrator in her late forties is sent the photographs from her niece’s wedding. Before she has looked at the bride she has found herself in every picture, and deleted three. Then she realises she has been doing this for thirty years. At church a widowed friend in her seventies says, laughing, “I wish I’d stopped grading myself sooner. I missed so many good days.” The administrator begins, very simply, to thank God each evening for one thing her body did that day: carried shopping, held a grandchild, climbed the hill.

What Christ says to her

Isaiah says of the coming Saviour, “he had no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him” (Isaiah 53:2). The Son of God took a body that would not have won any contest, and then he let it be marred for us on the cross. He did not come for the beautiful. He came for the loved, and made them lovely.

He looks at your heart, and then he gives you a new one. “Those who look to him are radiant, and their faces shall never be ashamed” (Psalm 34:5). Radiance comes from where you look, not how you look. And one day Christ “will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body” (Philippians 3:21). Every wrinkle is temporary. The glory is not.

For reflection

When do you most often find yourself grading your appearance? What half-truth makes the lie feel right to you? How does it change things to know that your adorning is “very precious” in God’s sight? What would it look like to thank God for your body this week rather than judge it?

2.title: “It All Depends on Me”
2.essay:
Two lies often travel together. One says, “I must be everything to everyone.” The other says, “If I don’t keep control, it will all fall apart.” The first says yes to everything. The second grips everything tightly. Both leave a woman exhausted, and strangely alone.

The lie in her own words

“If I don’t do it, no one will.” “I can’t say no, they’ll be so disappointed.” “If I stop checking, something terrible will happen.” You may hear it as the mother of small children, the daughter caring for an ageing parent, the nurse on a short-staffed ward, the friend everyone calls in a crisis, or the single woman whom everyone assumes has unlimited free time.

Why it is so believable

Again, there is truth in it. Love does serve. Scripture honours the woman whose “lamp does not go out at night” (Proverbs 31:18). Many women really do carry more than their share, and some things really would go undone without them. Responsibility is real.

But the lie moves quietly from “God has called me to serve” to “I am the one holding it all up.” It turns a calling into a weight no creature was made to carry. The study Busy, Tired & Restless looks at hurry, overwork and rest in general. Here we look at what the heart is trusting.

Martha’s question

When Jesus came to her home, “Martha was distracted with much serving” (Luke 10:40). She was not doing anything wrong. She was serving the Lord himself. But listen to what came out: “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone?” (Luke 10:40). When we believe everything depends on us, we often end up resenting others and doubting God’s care.

Jesus answered, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary” (Luke 10:41–42). He said her name twice, as you would to someone you love who is spinning. He did not tell her the meal was worthless. He invited her to sit down, and to receive before she gave.

Sarah’s plan

Sarah (still called Sarai) had waited ten years for the child God promised. Finally she took charge. “Behold now, the LORD has prevented me from bearing children. Go in to my servant; it may be that I shall obtain children by her” (Genesis 16:2). It was a custom of the day and seemed sensible, but it took the promise out of God’s hands.

It went badly, as control usually does. Hagar despised her. Sarah blamed her husband: “May the wrong done to me be on you!” (Genesis 16:5). And “Sarai dealt harshly with her” (Genesis 16:6), so that a pregnant servant fled into the desert. Control rarely stays contained. It often ends up hurting someone with less power than we have.

Yet look at God. He met Hagar by a spring, and she called him “a God of seeing” (Genesis 16:13). And years later he asked Sarah, “Is anything too hard for the LORD?” (Genesis 18:14). He had not been late. He did not need her plan. He was keeping his promise all along.

The God who does not sleep

“It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep” (Psalm 127:2). You can lie down at night because someone else stays awake: “Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep” (Psalm 121:4).

Even Jesus said no. Early one morning the disciples found him at prayer: “Everyone is looking for you” (Mark 1:37). He did not go back to the crowd. He went on to the next towns, because that was the work his Father had given him. Saying no is not unloving when it protects a yes to what God has actually asked of you. Paul says both “Bear one another’s burdens” (Galatians 6:2) and “each will have to bear his own load” (Galatians 6:5). You are called to help carry others. You are not called to carry everyone.

When saying no is not safe

If the pressure never to say no comes from someone who frightens, controls, threatens or hurts you, the problem is not your weak boundaries. That is abuse. Safety comes first: tell someone you trust, and contact the police or a domestic abuse helpline. God does not ask you to stay in danger. The study Biblical Counseling has a chapter on domestic violence and abuse.

An example

A mother of three works part-time, runs the church crèche and checks on her widowed neighbour daily. When she is asked to organise the harvest supper, her heart races. She hears herself say, “I’m sorry, I can’t this year.” Her hands shake afterwards. Nobody is upset. Someone else gladly takes it. That night, for the first time in weeks, she falls asleep without making a list.

What Christ says to her

“Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). He says “come to me”, not “do more for me”. The world was held together before you woke this morning, and it will be held together while you sleep, because “in him all things hold together” (Colossians 1:17). He has already carried the one load that would have crushed us all, our sin, to the cross. So Peter can write to every anxious Martha, “casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7). That is the answer to Martha’s question. He does care.

For reflection

Where in your life do you feel that everything depends on you? Is your struggle more with saying yes to everything, or with needing to control outcomes? What did Sarah’s plan cost, and whom did it hurt? What is one thing you could lay down this week, trusting the God who does not sleep?

3.title: “Not Enough, and Too Much”
3.essay:
Strangely, many women hear both at once. “I’m not enough”: not clever, organised, spiritual, interesting or attractive enough. And “I’m too much”: too emotional, too loud, too needy, too opinionated. Squeezed between the two, she concludes that she must earn love by getting herself exactly right.

The lie in her own words

“Other women manage. Why can’t I?” “I’d better not say how I really feel; it’ll put them off.” “If I’m more helpful, more cheerful, less trouble, they’ll want me around.” “God must be tired of me.” Beneath these sits a third lie that drives the other two: I have to earn love.

Why it is so believable

There is truth here too. In ourselves, none of us is enough. Paul says plainly, “Not that we are sufficient in ourselves … but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Corinthians 3:5). And sometimes we really are too much: sin can be loud, demanding and self-absorbed. But the lie offers the wrong cure. It says, “Manage yourself into being lovable.” Often it was learned young, from a parent who was hard to please, a home where feelings were unwelcome, or a friendship that was withdrawn without warning. The studies The Fear of Man and Perfectionism & Self-Condemnation look further at the need for approval and the inner critic.

Leah: never enough

Leah was the older sister, overshadowed from the start: “Leah’s eyes were weak, but Rachel was beautiful in form and appearance” (Genesis 29:17). Jacob married her only because he was tricked, and “he loved Rachel more than Leah” (Genesis 29:30).

The names Leah gave her sons read like a diary of trying to earn love. Reuben: “for now my husband will love me” (Genesis 29:32). Levi: “Now this time my husband will be attached to me” (Genesis 29:34). Each child was another attempt to become enough. It did not work.

But the Bible tells us something Leah may not have felt: “When the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb” (Genesis 29:31). God saw her. And with her fourth son something changed. She said, “This time I will praise the LORD” (Genesis 29:35), and named him Judah. From Judah came King David, and from David came Christ. The unloved wife became a mother in the line of the Saviour.

Hannah and the woman with the flask: too much

Hannah prayed so intensely that the priest thought she was drunk. She answered him, “Do not regard your servant as a worthless woman, for all along I have been speaking out of my great anxiety and vexation” (1 Samuel 1:16). To Eli she looked like too much. God heard her prayer.

In Bethany a woman broke a flask of costly ointment over Jesus’ head. The guests thought it extravagant, a waste, far too much, “And they scolded her. But Jesus said, ‘Leave her alone. Why do you trouble her? She has done a beautiful thing to me’” (Mark 14:5–6). Not every strong feeling is holy, and love does sometimes ask us to be quieter. But Jesus is not embarrassed by a woman’s tears, devotion or longing. What others called too much, he called beautiful.

Love that is not earned

The gospel does not say, “Become lovable, and God will love you.” It says, “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). “In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 4:10). God’s love came first, at its highest cost, to people who had done nothing to earn it.

God even uses a mother’s love as the lesser picture: “Can a woman forget her nursing child …? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you. Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands” (Isaiah 49:15–16). And Zephaniah describes a God who is, if anything, the one who is “too much” in love: “he will rejoice over you with gladness; he will quiet you by his love; he will exult over you with loud singing” (Zephaniah 3:17). He does not quiet you by asking you to shrink. He quiets you by loving you.

An example

A solicitor in her thirties, single, rereads every message three times before sending it, trimming anything that sounds too keen or too cold. In her home group she rarely speaks. One evening she disagrees with something, says so, then apologises at once. Afterwards a friend says, “I liked it when you said what you thought. Please don’t stop.” At home she reads Zephaniah 3:17 and realises that God has never been measuring her volume.

What Christ says to her

Christ does not say, “You are enough.” He says something better: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). You do not need to be enough, because he is. And he is never overwhelmed by you. “For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses” (Hebrews 4:15). Your feelings, needs and questions are not too much for the one who carried the sin of the world. Like Leah, you can stop naming your days after the love you are trying to win, and start naming them after the Lord who already loves you.

For reflection

Do you more often hear “not enough” or “too much”, and from whose voice? What have you done, like Leah, to try to earn love? What does Mark 14:6 tell you about how Jesus sees wholehearted devotion? How would your week change if you believed God rejoices over you with singing?

4.title: “My Past Disqualifies Me”
4.essay:
Some women believe that God has forgiven them, but that the past still bars the door. Heaven, perhaps; usefulness, no. “Other women can lead a Bible study, pray aloud, speak to a friend about Jesus. Not me. Not after what I’ve done.”

The lie in her own words

The past may be an abortion, an affair, years of living far from God, an addiction, a divorce, a reputation in a small town that never quite fades. Or it may be something done to her, which she still feels as a stain even though it was not her sin. Either way, the lie says: God may let me in, but I will always be second-rate in his family.

Why it is so believable

Sin has consequences, and some of them remain. Trust broken takes time to rebuild. Scripture does weigh a person’s life for some responsibilities, such as eldership. But the lie turns consequences into a verdict. It says that what you did, or what was done to you, has fixed your place in God’s family for ever, somewhere near the back.

The study Shame deals with the feeling of being “something wrong”, and Regret & the Past with decisions that cannot be undone. This chapter asks a narrower question: does your past keep you from belonging fully and being used by God?

Rahab

Rahab was a Canaanite and a prostitute in Jericho, a city under God’s judgment. Yet she heard what God had done for Israel and believed: “for the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath” (Joshua 2:11). She hid the spies at risk to her life, and when the city fell, “Rahab the prostitute and her father’s household and all who belonged to her, Joshua saved alive. And she has lived in Israel to this day” (Joshua 6:25).

The New Testament does not forget her. She stands in the great list of faith: “By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient” (Hebrews 11:31). Notice that the old label stays. It is not kept to shame her. It is kept to show how great God’s grace is. And Matthew writes her into the family tree of Jesus himself: “Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab” (Matthew 1:5). God did not merely forgive Rahab’s past. He put her name in his Son’s genealogy.

The woman in Simon’s house

Luke tells of “a woman of the city, who was a sinner” (Luke 7:37) who came into a Pharisee’s dinner, wept over Jesus’ feet, wiped them with her hair and anointed them. The host thought, “If this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him” (Luke 7:39).

Jesus turned to her and asked Simon, “Do you see this woman?” (Luke 7:44). Simon saw a category. Jesus saw a woman. Then he said, “her sins, which are many, are forgiven … for she loved much” (Luke 7:47). Her many sins did not limit her love. Forgiven, they became the measure of it. And he spoke to her directly: “Your faith has saved you; go in peace” (Luke 7:50).

Washed, not patched

Paul lists serious sins and then writes, “And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11). Notice the past tense: such were some of you. In Christ your past is not your present identity. “Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come” (2 Corinthians 5:17).

Paul himself had persecuted the church. Far from disqualifying him, his past became a display of grace: “I received mercy for this reason, that in me, as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe in him” (1 Timothy 1:16). Your story, told honestly, may be exactly what another woman needs to hear.

What was done to you

If your past includes abuse or assault, hear this clearly: what was done to you was sin against you. It is not your guilt, and it does not disqualify you from anything. If you are in any danger now, safety comes first: tell someone you trust and contact the police. The study Shame speaks gently about shame put on us by others.

An example

A woman in her fifties, divorced after an affair she deeply regrets, sat at the back of church for years, slipping out before the last hymn. When an older woman asked her to help with a group for young mothers, she said, “You don’t know what I’ve done.” The older woman replied, “I know enough. I also know what Christ has done.” Two years later a young wife whose marriage was in trouble found that the woman from the back row understood her better than anyone.

What Christ says to her

He says what he said in Simon’s house: “Your sins are forgiven” (Luke 7:48). He says what God said through Isaiah: “though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow” (Isaiah 1:18). The blood of the Son of God is not a partial payment that leaves you on probation. It is enough to wash you completely, and to seat you at the table as a daughter, not a servant. “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Go in peace.

For reflection

Is there something in your past that you feel bars you from serving God? What does it mean to you that Rahab is named in the genealogy of Jesus? Jesus asked, “Do you see this woman?” How do you think he sees you? Is there someone whose story is like yours whom your story might help?

5.title: “Second-Class, and Not Yet Complete”
5.essay:
Two lies concern being a woman in God’s world. One says, “God’s plan for women makes me second-class.” The other says, “I won’t be complete without a husband or children,” or, for some married women, “My marriage is who I am.” Both make a woman smaller than God made her.

The first lie in her own words

“God prefers men.” “My gifts are wasted in the church.” “Women are an afterthought.” Many believe it because of how they have been treated. It must be said honestly: some church cultures have spoken of women with contempt, ignored their gifts or used Scripture to silence them. That is sin, against them and against the Bible itself.

Equal from the beginning

“So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27). The woman is not a lesser copy. She bears God’s image fully. When God calls her “a helper fit for him” (Genesis 2:18), he uses a word the Old Testament often uses of God himself: “My help comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth” (Psalm 121:2). Helper is not a junior word. Peter tells husbands that their wives are “heirs with you of the grace of life” (1 Peter 3:7), and Paul says that in Christ “there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28).

Jesus and the women who followed him

Women travelled with Jesus and the twelve, “who provided for them out of their means” (Luke 8:3). Women stayed at the cross, and were the first witnesses of the resurrection, in a world where their testimony was often discounted: “it was Mary Magdalene and Joanna and Mary the mother of James and the other women with them who told these things to the apostles” (Luke 24:10). The first word of the risen Lord to any disciple, in John’s account, was a woman’s name: “Mary” (John 20:16).

Paul’s letters are full of women in the work: Phoebe, “a servant of the church at Cenchreae” and “a patron of many” (Romans 16:1–2); Prisca, one of Paul’s “fellow workers in Christ Jesus” (Romans 16:3); and Junia, “well known to the apostles” (Romans 16:7). The study Biblical Womanhood tells their stories more fully.

The question of roles

Christians who love the Bible differ over what women may do in marriage and the church. Egalitarians believe Galatians 3:28 and the ministry of women like Junia and Phoebe show that every role and office is open to men and women alike, reading 1 Timothy 2 as answering a local problem. Complementarians believe men and women are equal in worth but given different callings: the husband’s headship, exercised in Christ’s self-giving love, and the eldership and authoritative teaching of the gathered church, entrusted to qualified men. They note that Paul grounds this in creation, and read Galatians 3:28 as being about our standing before God rather than our roles. Both sides insist that women are fully equal in worth.

This commentary’s view: We hold the complementarian view, and we hold it gently. Difference of role is not difference of worth: “the head of Christ is God” (1 Corinthians 11:3), yet the Son is not less than the Father. Most of what God calls women to do, praying, learning, teaching in many settings, serving, giving, leading, evangelising and shaping the next generation, is shared ground with men. Headship never permits harshness, control or abuse, and any teaching used to belittle women misuses Scripture.

The second lie: “I won’t be complete”

“My life will start when I marry.” “I’m a failure because I can’t have children.” “Without him, who am I?” Marriage and children are good gifts, and longing for them is not sin: “Hope deferred makes the heart sick” (Proverbs 13:12). But they cannot make anyone complete.

Once a woman in the crowd cried out to Jesus, “Blessed is the womb that bore you” (Luke 11:27). He answered, “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it!” (Luke 11:28). The greatest blessing is open to every woman. To those who seemed to have no future in a family line God promised “a name better than sons and daughters” (Isaiah 56:5). In Christ, “you have been filled in him” (Colossians 2:10). Jesus himself lived his whole life unmarried. The study Singleness explores this, and Disappointment & Waiting speaks to those who long for what has not come.

For married women the danger is different: a good marriage can quietly become an identity. But marriage is a picture, not the whole. “In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage” (Matthew 22:30), because the marriage it pointed to will have come: “the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready” (Revelation 19:7). Widows, too, are not left without a protector: “For your Maker is your husband” (Isaiah 54:5).

An example

For forty years a woman was known as “his wife”. After her husband’s funeral she cannot fill in a form without crying at the word “widowed”. Months later, helping at a church lunch, she finds gifts no one noticed while she stood beside him: she remembers names, and she listens. She is still his widow. But she discovers, slowly, that before she was anyone’s wife she was God’s daughter, and she still is.

What Christ says to her

He calls her by name, as he called Mary in the garden. He sends her with good news, as he sent the women from the tomb. He gives her a fullness no husband or child could give, and he promises that every woman who trusts him belongs to his Bride, whom he loved and gave himself for. In his kingdom she is neither second-class nor half a person. She is his.

For reflection

Have you ever felt second-class as a woman in the church? Where did that feeling come from? How do the women at the empty tomb speak to that feeling? Which have you been tempted to make your identity: marriage, children, or their absence? What does it mean to you that in Christ you “have been filled in him”?

6.title: Truth for Every Day
6.essay:
Lies are rarely defeated once and for all. They come back on tired evenings, in waiting rooms, on anniversaries, in the middle of the night. So this last chapter is practical. But first one more lie needs naming, because it quietly powers all the others: my feelings are the truth.

“My feelings are the truth”

It sounds like this: “I feel worthless, so I must be.” “I feel God is far away, so he is.” “I feel guilty, so I can’t be forgiven.” Feelings are real, and God made them. The Psalms are full of them, honestly expressed. But feelings are messengers, not masters. They tell us what is happening in us. They do not always tell us what is true about us.

The psalmist shows another way. Instead of only listening to his soul, he speaks to it: “Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him” (Psalm 42:5). Scripture warns, “The heart is deceitful above all things” (Jeremiah 17:9), and it comforts: “whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything” (1 John 3:20). Feelings usually follow truth, but slowly. Keep telling yourself the truth while you wait for them.

Renewing the mind

“Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind” (Romans 12:2). Lies are often habits of thought worn deep by years, replaced not by one good sermon but by the slow work of the Spirit through the word. Paul speaks of taking “every thought captive to obey Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:5). In practice that means three small steps. Catch the thought: notice the sentence running in your head. Check it: is this true, according to God? Change it: answer it with what he says.

That is what Jesus did when the devil lied to him in the wilderness. Each time he answered, “It is written” (Matthew 4:4). He did not argue with his feelings. He quoted his Father. You might write the lies from this study on one side of a page, and beside each the verses that answer it. Keep it where you will see it: by the kettle, in your bag, on your phone.

Choose what you dwell on

“Whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is commendable, if there is any excellence, if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things” (Philippians 4:8). This is not positive thinking. It is true thinking. Notice what feeds the lies, and what feeds the truth: Scripture, worship, honest friends, the Lord’s Day with God’s people.

Women among women

Paul tells Titus that older women “are to teach what is good, and so train the young women” (Titus 2:3–4). God means women to help one another into the truth. A single woman of seventy and a young mother, a widow and a student, a woman in an office and a woman at home: each knows things the others need. Look for a woman a little further along the road, and be one for someone else. This is “exhort one another every day” (Hebrews 3:13) in ordinary clothes. The study Friendship & Hospitality has more.

Every morning

You may have to answer the same lie a hundred times. That is not failure. “The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness” (Lamentations 3:22–23). Each morning there is new mercy for the old battle.

When you need more help

Sometimes these lies grow into something more. If you are struggling with food, weight or your body, please see a doctor; the study Eating Disorders will help. If you have felt low for weeks and cannot lift it, see your doctor; Depression & the Christian is written for you. Seeing a doctor or a qualified counsellor, or taking prescribed medicine, is not a failure of faith.

If you are harming yourself, or thinking about ending your life, please get help now. Call the emergency services (999 or 112 in the UK and Europe, 911 in North America) or a crisis line (Samaritans on 116 123 in the UK and Ireland, 988 in the United States), and tell someone you trust. Your life is precious to God.

If someone at home frightens, controls or hurts you, safety comes first. Contact the police or a domestic abuse helpline, and tell a trusted person. The study Biblical Counseling has chapters on abuse and on self-harm.

An example

A young mother at home with two small children notices that by mid-afternoon the same voice comes every day: “You’re failing at this. Everyone else copes.” She writes it on a sticky note, and underneath, “My grace is sufficient for you” (2 Corinthians 12:9). Then she texts an older friend from church: “Bad afternoon. Pray?” The reply comes within minutes. The voice has not disappeared. But it no longer gets the last word.

Further reading

Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth’s book Lies Women Believe covers similar ground at greater length.

The truth is a Person

In the end you are not fighting lies with slogans. You are listening to a voice. Jesus said, “The sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name” (John 10:3). Every lie in this study is answered, finally, by who he is and what he has done: the Son who carried every load, welcomed the woman with a past, and called a woman by name on the first Easter morning. “So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed” (John 8:36).

For reflection

Which lie from this study do you most need to answer every day? What verse will you use to answer it? Who is an older woman you could learn from, or a younger woman you could encourage? Is there any sign in your life that you need more help than a study can give, and whom will you tell?
